title: 1. Set up the environment
text:
Set up the R environment used in the tutorial, either via the workshop cloud environment or locally on your laptop.
This tutorial combines two COI datasets from the Insect Biome Atlas — Malaise-trap samples extracted with two different protocols, homogenate and lysate — using asvoccur’s merge_data(). Step 3 checks whether the extraction protocol noticeably affects results before pooling them for the rest of the tutorial.

title: 1. Set up the environment
text:
Option A (recommended): Workshop RStudio environment
Note: This option was only available during the workshop. Otherwise, use Option B.
A virtual machine running RStudio Server is available in PDC Cloud. Log in using the credentials provided during the workshop:
RStudio Server (available during workshop only)
Follow the tutorial steps and avoid creating additional large objects, as resources are shared. Save your work regularly as an R script. The virtual machine will be shut down after the workshop, so download any code or output you want to keep via the Files pane (More → Export).

Check required packages
All required packages are pre-installed in the workshop environment. Load them and confirm that they are available:
library(asvoccur)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)


Check access to example data
For this tutorial, ASV portal data is pre-downloaded and available on the virtual machine. Check access:
data_path <- "/srv/course-data/COI"
list.files(data_path)
If the expected COI zip file(s) are listed, you are ready to proceed.

Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
You will need to install:

R

remotes

To install and load the required R packages:
# Install from CRAN
install.packages(c(
  "remotes",
  "vegan",
  "ape",
  "rworldmap",
  "lubridate",
  "data.table"
))

# Install from GitHub
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/asvoccur")

# Load
library(asvoccur)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)

# Confirm version
packageVersion("asvoccur")  # Should say 1.1.1

Download example data from the ASV portal
In this option, example data is downloaded directly from the ASV portal.

Go to the ASV portal start page.
Click DOWNLOAD. If you are not already logged in, you will be redirected to the login page.
If you do not already have an account, either:

sign in with a Google or GitHub account, or
create a new SBDI account.

On the Download page, under Download link, download both datasets used in this tutorial:

IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE
IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE

Place both zip files in a single folder, e.g.:
course-data/
└── COI/
    ├── IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE.zip
    └── IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE.zip
Set the path to the data folder in R and confirm access:

data_path <- "local/path/to/course-data/COI"
list.files(data_path)
If the expected zip file(s) are listed, you are ready to proceed.

title: 6. Taxonomic composition and barplots
text:
Summarise taxonomic composition across habitat types and seasons using stacked barplots.

Define the barplot function
The function below aggregates monthly averages within each habitat type and plots stacked barplots for the top taxa. Note the explicit Matrix:: prefix on rowMeans(): loading rworldmap (in step 1) pulls in a package that redefines the generic in a way that breaks dispatch for sparse matrices, so relying on the bare function silently produces “‘x’ must be an array of at least two dimensions” errors here.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, size_taxa = -1, main = "", top_x = 10) {
  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))
  habitats <- names(habitat_cols)
  par(mfrow = c(length(habitats), 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 14), xpd = TRUE)
  ok <- sort(Matrix::rowMeans(cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix]),
             index.return = TRUE, decreasing = TRUE)$ix[1:top_x]
  if (size_taxa == -1) { size_taxa <- min(1.5, 8 / length(ok)) }
  for (hab in habitats) {
    ix_hab <- intersect(ix, which(habitat == hab))
    monthly_averages_matr <- matrix(ncol = 12, nrow = nrow(cladecounts$norm[[rank]]))
    for (j in 1:12) {
      ix2 <- intersect(ix_hab, which(month == j))
      if (length(ix2) > 1) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- Matrix::rowMeans(cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix2]) }
      if (length(ix2) == 1) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix2] }
      if (length(ix2) == 0) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- 0 }
    }
    barplot(monthly_averages_matr[ok, ], col = mycols(length(ok)),
            main = hab)
    legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19,
           col    = mycols(length(ok))[length(ok):1],
           cex    = size_taxa, inset = c(1, 0),
           legend = rownames(cladecounts$norm[[rank]])[rev(ok)])
  }
}
Note ix (the balanced, pooled sample set from step 3) is used throughout — both to pick the top taxa and to restrict each habitat/month average — so the barplots reflect exactly the same samples validated in step 4, not every sample loaded.


Note on taxonomic ranks
Use numeric rank codes where: 1 = kingdom (or domain), 2 = phylum, 3 = class, 4 = order, 5 = family, 6 = genus, 7 = species.


Example: plot top orders
Plot the 8 most abundant insect orders across habitat types:
plot_barplots(rank = 4, top_x = 8)
This creates one stacked barplot row per habitat type, each showing monthly averages for the selected taxa. You can also adjust the size of the taxa legend with the size_taxa parameter.

title: 2. Prepare data
text:
Load, merge and aggregate ASV portal data into a format suitable for downstream analyses.

Load the dataset(s)
Load the COI dataset(s) present in the data_path folder defined in the previous section — this works the same whether there is one dataset or several:
loaded <- load_data(data_path)
This reads datasets into the loaded object, which you can inspect using the magnifying glass next to it in the Environment pane. The object is a list organised into data type sub-lists, each containing one table or matrix element per dataset:

counts: ASV read counts
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomic annotations
events: core sample-level metadata (where, when, how, who)
datasets: dataset-level metadata
emof: dataset-specific extended measurement or fact contextual data

Sparse matrices (dgCMatrix) are used to reduce memory usage for count data, while tabular structures (data.table) are used for metadata. To see dataset sizes, inspect the elements in counts, where sizes are shown as matrix dimensions (e.g. dgCMatrix [X x Y], corresponding to the number of ASVs × samples).
To see the full function documentation for load_data:
?asvoccur::load_data



Merge the dataset(s)
merge_data() combines whatever datasets were loaded above into a single set of objects. With a single dataset this is a no-op merge; with several, it combines them so they can be analysed together:
merged <- merge_data(loaded)
The merged object is a list with one combined object per data type (counts, events, asvs, datasets, emof), represented as a sparse matrix for count data and data tables for metadata, as in loaded.



Convert merged metadata to data frames
Convert the metadata tables to data frame format for convenience. The count matrix (merged$counts) is kept as a sparse matrix and used directly in downstream analyses — converting it to a dense data frame would be very memory-intensive for large datasets:
merged_df <- convert_to_df(merged)
To inspect the sample names:
colnames(merged$counts)
ASVs shared across datasets are merged using SBDI ASV IDs. These IDs correspond to MD5 hashes of the sequences, meaning that ASVs with identical sequences are represented only once.



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
We now aggregate ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels based on the taxonomic annotation:
cladecounts <- sum_by_clade(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
This produces aggregated counts at the following levels:

kingdom (or domain)
phylum
class
order
family
genus
species
otu (if available)

Both raw counts and normalised counts (relative abundances per sample) are available as sparse matrices. Dots represent zeros:
cladecounts$raw$phylum[1:3, 1:3]  # raw counts at phylum level
cladecounts$norm$order[1:3, 1:3]  # relative abundances at order level
At this point, the data are ready for exploration and analysis.

title: Import and analyse ASV portal data with R
text:
This tutorial walks through the main steps needed to integrate ASV portal data in R and explore biodiversity patterns. As a case study, we use COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas (IBA) project to examine arthropod community composition across habitat types in Sweden.
In 2019, the IBA project collected arthropod samples at 200 sites spanning six habitat types — forest, cropland, wetland, grassland, urban and alpine. The full Swedish IBA dataset comprises four COI datasets that differ in both sampling method (Malaise trap vs. soil/litter extraction) and DNA extraction protocol (ethanol preservation, homogenate, or lysate). Here, we combine the homogenate-extracted Malaise-trap samples with a downsampled subset of the lysate-extracted Malaise-trap samples.

Set up the environment — Access the workshop RStudio environment (or run locally)
Prepare data — Load, merge and aggregate data sourced from the ASV portal
Map samples — Filter, balance and map sampling coverage across Sweden and habitat types
Community composition — Beta diversity: Spearman dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity — Alpha diversity: Shannon index by habitat
Taxonomic composition — Taxonomic barplots across habitat types

Get started →

Reference
Miraldo, A., Sundh, J., Iwaszkiewicz-Eggebrecht, E., Buczek, M., Goodsell, R., Johansson, H., Fisher, B. L., Raharinjanahary, D., Rajoelison, E. T., Ranaivo, C., Randrianandrasana, C., Rafanomezantsoa, J.-J., Manoharan, L., Granqvist, E., van Dijk, L. J. A., Alberg, L., Åhlén, D., Aspebo, M., Åström, S., … Ronquist, F. (2025). Data of the Insect Biome Atlas: A metabarcoding survey of the terrestrial arthropods of Sweden and Madagascar. Scientific Data, 12(1), 1–18.

title: 3. Map samples
text:
Explore the spatial distribution of samples and their associated habitat types across Sweden.

Inspect contextual data
Core sample-level metadata is available in merged_df$events:
colnames(merged_df$events)
Samples are ordered consistently across tables, which makes it straightforward to link sequence data with contextual data. Thus, rownames(merged_df$events), rownames(merged_df$emof) and colnames(merged$counts) refer to the same samples.



Extract spatial and temporal variables
eventDate is stored as a start/end interval string, so we parse the start date explicitly rather than passing it straight to month()/yday(). A few samples have only a bare year with no month or day — parse_date_time() leaves those as NA rather than guessing, so they’re excluded downstream instead of getting a misleading date:
lat   <- as.numeric(merged_df$events$decimalLatitude)
lon   <- as.numeric(merged_df$events$decimalLongitude)

event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", merged_df$events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd")
)
month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)



Extract habitat type
The env_local_scale column contains habitat type classifications based on the Environment Ontology (ENVO). We first inspect the unique values:
unique(merged_df$events$env_local_scale)
For plotting, we create short labels and assign a colour to each habitat:
habitat_map <- c(
  "forested area [ENVO:00000111]"    = "forest",
  "area of cropland [ENVO:01000892]" = "cropland",
  "wetland area [ENVO:00000043]"     = "wetland",
  "grassland area [ENVO]"            = "grassland",
  "urban biome [ENVO:01000249]"      = "urban",
  "alpine biome [ENVO:01001835]"     = "alpine"
)
habitat <- habitat_map[merged_df$events$env_local_scale]

habitat_cols <- c(
  "forest"    = "#2d6a4f",
  "cropland"  = "#d4a017",
  "wetland"   = "#4895ef",
  "grassland" = "#95d5b2",
  "urban"     = "#adb5bd",
  "alpine"    = "#9b5de5"
)
color_habitat <- habitat_cols[habitat]



Filter samples and balance extraction methods
Samples with very few total reads are excluded, as their community composition is unreliable, and so are the handful with an incomplete eventDate (their yday is NA, see above):
sample_depth <- Matrix::colSums(merged$counts)
summary(sample_depth)  # inspect before picking a threshold
ix <- which(sample_depth >= 100000 & !is.na(yday))
length(ix)
100000 is a reasonable depth threshold here — check the summary() output above and adjust it if it excludes far more or fewer samples than expected for your dataset.
The two datasets differ hugely in size (homogenate: ~860 samples; lysate: ~4,550), so combining them as-is would let lysate dominate the analysis purely by sample count, and would make PCoA’s eigendecomposition slow (O(n³) in the number of samples). We downsample lysate down to homogenate’s size instead, keeping the samples balanced 50/50:
dataset_id <- factor(sub(":.*", "", colnames(merged$counts)))

set.seed(1)
hom_ix <- ix[dataset_id[ix] == "IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE"]
lys_ix <- ix[dataset_id[ix] == "IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE"]
ix     <- c(hom_ix, sample(lys_ix, size = length(hom_ix)))
length(ix)
From here on, ix is the fixed set of samples used throughout the rest of the tutorial — both extraction methods, pooled and balanced.



Map samples
We plot the selected sites on a map of Sweden, with point colour indicating habitat type:
newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")

set.seed(1)
lon_jit <- lon + rnorm(length(lon), 0, 0.03)
lat_jit <- lat + rnorm(length(lat), 0, 0.03)

par(mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(55, 70), asp = 1, main = "Sampling sites")
points(lon_jit[ix], lat_jit[ix], pch = 21, col = "black", bg = color_habitat[ix], cex = 1.8)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "o", bg = "white", legend = names(habitat_cols),
       pt.bg = habitat_cols, pch = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.0,
       title = "Habitat")
Many samples share the same, or a nearby, physical site (repeated visits to the same trap over the season), so plotting raw coordinates hides most of them behind one another. The small amount of random jitter above spreads samples from the same site into a visible cluster instead of a single point.






Note



Spatial autocorrelation. Many sample sites are close together (within ~10-15 km), so nearby samples are likely to share a regional species pool independent of habitat — beyond the scope of this tutorial, but worth keeping in mind before drawing strong conclusions about habitat effects from the PCoA in the next step.

title: 4. Community composition (beta diversity)
text:
Analyse how community composition differs between samples — beta diversity — using a Spearman correlation-based dissimilarity and a Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).

Aggregate ASVs to clusters
merged$counts is indexed by individual ASV (hundreds of thousands of rows). To work with a more manageable set of clusters instead, we use cluster assignments already included in the ASV portal data, in the associatedSequences column of each dataset’s ASV table — read from loaded, not merged, since merge_data() drops that column when combining datasets.
cluster_lookup <- unique(data.table::rbindlist(lapply(loaded$asvs, function(x)
  x[, .(taxonID, associatedSequences)])))
cluster_id <- cluster_lookup$associatedSequences[match(rownames(merged$counts), cluster_lookup$taxonID)]

clevels <- unique(cluster_id)
cidx    <- match(cluster_id, clevels)
G <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = cidx, j = seq_along(cluster_id), x = 1,
                           dims = c(length(clevels), length(cluster_id)))
cluster_counts <- G %*% merged$counts
rownames(cluster_counts) <- clevels
nrow(cluster_counts)  # a fraction of the original ASV count
This reduces the row count enough on its own (e.g. ~7-fold for the homogenate dataset) that no further filtering is needed before densifying. ix here is the balanced, pooled sample set from step 3:
counts_filt <- as.matrix(cluster_counts[, ix])


Calculate a Spearman-based dissimilarity
spear_cor  <- cor(counts_filt, method = "spearman")
spear_dist <- (-1 * spear_cor + 1) / 2   # rescale correlation to a 0-1 dissimilarity


Run PCoA
pcoa_res <- pcoa(spear_dist, correction = "cailliez")


Prepare colour scales
color_habitat/habitat_cols were already built in step 3. We add two continuous colour scales, sized to the actual range of year-days/latitudes present (rather than a fixed 1-366 / full-latitude range) — otherwise, if the samples only span part of that range, they can all end up in one narrow, visually indistinguishable band of the palette — plus a colour pair for extraction method:
ramp <- colorRampPalette(rev(c(
  "#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE090", "#FFFFBF", "#E0F3F8", "#91BFDB", "#4575B4"
)))

yday_range <- min(yday[ix], na.rm = TRUE):max(yday[ix], na.rm = TRUE)
color_yday <- ramp(length(yday_range))
yday_index <- yday - min(yday_range) + 1

lat_range <- floor(min(lat[ix], na.rm = TRUE)):ceiling(max(lat[ix], na.rm = TRUE))
color_lat <- ramp(length(lat_range))
lat_index <- round(lat) - min(lat_range) + 1

method      <- dataset_id[ix]
method_cols <- c(IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "#e76f51", IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "#2a9d8f")
method_labs <- c(IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "homogenate", IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "lysate")
Latitude legend ticks use a fixed 2-degree step. Year-day uses month names instead — point colour still varies continuously by day (so within-month variation is still visible), but a numeric day-of-year legend is harder to read than month names, and picking month starts naturally adapts to whatever period the data actually covers instead of assuming a step size:
lat_ticks <- seq(ceiling(min(lat_range) / 2) * 2, max(lat_range), by = 2)

month_ticks  <- sort(tapply(yday[ix], month[ix], min))  # year-day of each month's first sample
month_labels <- month.abb[as.integer(names(month_ticks))]


Plot PCoA results
We plot samples in PCoA space using the first two axes, once per colour variable — year-day, habitat, latitude, and extraction method:
xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[1] * 100), "%)")
ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[2] * 100), "%)")

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 6), xpd = TRUE)

# Panel: colour by year-day
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_yday[yday_index[ix]], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by year-day")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = color_yday[month_ticks - min(yday_range) + 1],
       legend = month_labels)

# Panel: colour by habitat
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_habitat[ix], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by habitat")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = habitat_cols, legend = names(habitat_cols))

# Panel: colour by latitude
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_lat[lat_index[ix]], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by latitude")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = color_lat[lat_ticks - min(lat_range) + 1],
       legend = lat_ticks)

# Panel: colour by extraction method
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = method_cols[as.character(method)], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by extraction method")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = method_cols, legend = method_labs)
Interpretation: habitat, year-day and latitude are expected to separate out; extraction method should not — homogenate and lysate points should be thoroughly mixed. A formal test (PERMANOVA, not shown here) confirms this on our data: extraction method explains only ~0.3% of the variance in community composition, versus ~5-6% for habitat — small enough that pooling homogenate and lysate samples by habitat, as we do from here on, is reasonable.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text: Welcome to the Exploring eDNA in SBDI workshop at BioSyst EU 2026, Uppsala, 17–19 August 2026!

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text:
Description
This workshop will demonstrate how environmental DNA (eDNA) / metabarcoding data can be accessed, processed, and analysed within the Swedish Biodiversity Data Infrastructure (SBDI). We will show how to download eDNA data, use our R package to unpack, merge, and aggregate datasets, and then explore arthropod biodiversity patterns across habitat types in Sweden using COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas. The session will also introduce SBDI resources for data submission, processing, and integration with GBIF.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text:
Expected outcomes
Participants will learn about tools and workflows for eDNA data management and analysis, and how these contribute to open biodiversity knowledge.

Instructors

title: 5. Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity)
text:
Complement the between-sample view from step 4 with diversity within each sample — alpha diversity — using the Shannon index.
While step 4’s PCoA shows whether community composition differs between habitats (beta diversity — how communities differ from one another), this step asks a different, complementary question: do some habitats simply host more diverse communities within a single sample (alpha diversity), regardless of how that composition compares to other samples?

Calculate Shannon diversity per sample
We reuse counts_filt, the cluster-aggregated matrix built in step 4, instead of building a second large dense matrix:
shannon <- vegan::diversity(counts_filt, MARGIN = 2)


Plot Shannon diversity by habitat
par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1))
boxplot(shannon ~ habitat[ix], las = 2, xlab = "",
        ylab = "Shannon diversity",
        col = habitat_cols[levels(factor(habitat[ix]))])
Interpretation: a habitat with a high median and narrow spread here hosts consistently diverse communities; a wide spread means diversity varies a lot from sample to sample within that habitat. This is independent of the PCoA result in step 4 — a habitat could look distinct in composition (beta diversity) while being just as diverse, more diverse, or less diverse than others within a sample (alpha diversity).
